doc.title: Kent Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

title: Composing, arranging and analysis
summary: He sees himself more as an analyst and arranger; analysis (e.g. Brahms Clarinet Quintet, Coltrane solos) must be joined to emotion.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You do a certain amount of composing?

Actually what I’ve been doing lately has been — I’m not really a writer in that sense but I’m sort of like a person who likes to analyze music a lot. I think sometimes we get lost in the nomenclature. Analysis is very important. I think if you can analyze then you can compose. For me right now I’m finding that arranging, analyzing and practicing certain things — I mean it’s like certain devices that I know that work, that will work. And so the thing is to take those things that you know work and put them into some kind of musical context that will make it seem seamless. What I mean by that is for instance if you listen to Brahms, let’s say you’re listening to the “Clarinet Quintet.” And that music is really © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

perfect, I mean perfection. And when you really start — and then sometimes, in other words, you analyze them and you say why is this fitting like this? Why is this — but at the same time it’s still emotional, you know what I mean? In other words it’s not just a bunch of notes thrown on the paper and he knows how the violin, the cello and the viola and all these things interact but how do you make music from these things? And they get lost in it. I mean that’s what’s interesting to me. Like if you’re analyzing like a John Coltrane solo and you get all of the notes, everything is lining up, but there was something very emotional about it. And then at the same time there’s something very analytical about it. And so how do you bring those two things together so that they’re very seamless. And that’s what I try to convey to my students, I say you know you really have to deal with emotion but you also have to deal with the analysis. The analysis is very important. Don’t get too far away from the analysis.
